listenings.text: I run business development for a payments company, and I've learned one hard lesson about conferences. The deals are not lost at the event. They're lost in the three weeks after it. Here's my rule. You have seventy-two hours. In the first three days, people still remember meeting you, and a short message feels natural. After two weeks, the same message feels strange. So on the plane home, I make a simple list: every person, one next step, and a date. Then I send short messages, never long ones. Three lines, one clear question. And if somebody doesn't answer, I don't give up. I try sending something useful instead, like an article or a warm introduction to someone they should meet. That's how a dormant lead comes back to life.

Hi Fabio, it's Priya Nair from Clearline, the fintech from the startup area at Sibos. I hope the trip home was good. I'm calling because I remember talking to you about real-time settlement for trade finance, and I promised to send you our pilot results. They're ready now, and I've just emailed them to you. I also wanted to ask you something. Would it make sense to set up a short call with your innovation team in the next two weeks? I know these things can easily fall through the cracks after a big event, so I thought a quick call might help. Thanks, and talk soon.

reading.rtitle: The 72-Hour Window: Why Deals Die After Conferences
paras: Every big conference creates hundreds of new contacts. A few weeks later, most of them are dormant leads. The people were interested, the conversations were good, but nobody took the next step. In the busy weeks after the event, the opportunity simply fell through the cracks.

Experienced bankers know that the first seventy-two hours are the most valuable. People still remember meeting you, and a short message feels natural. Many of them make a list on the plane home: every person, one next step, and a date. That list becomes the new deal pipeline.

The best follow-ups are short. They start with one clear memory of the conversation, offer one useful thing, and end with one easy question. A long email full of slides is not a touchpoint; it is homework for the other person.

When a contact goes quiet, the answer is not to give up, and not to send the same message again. A polite nudge with an article, or a warm introduction to someone they should meet, is often enough for re-engagement.

Finally, a good banker manages several threads at the same time: a vendor, a partner bank, and the internal team. A simple stakeholder map shows who matters in each decision, and a clear escalation path shows where to go when a thread stops moving. That is how you keep a relationship warm long after the conference is over.
